title: Where is thy sting (1 Corinthians 15:51–57)
hookLine: O death, where is thy victory

lines: SOME SAY THE DEAD DON'T RISE.
AN ARGUMENT TURNS INTO A SONG.
cards: Some people in Corinth had decided the dead don't rise. Souls might go on, they thought, but bodies? Bodies rot.
Paul answers them in chapter fifteen, and it's an argument most of the way through: he reasons, lists the people who saw the risen Christ, talks about seeds and harvest.
Then, near the end, the argument turns into something more like a song. He starts taunting death itself, as if it were a bully that's finally been beaten.

teach.h: A MYSTERY: WE SHALL BE CHANGED.
teach.b: He begins with a secret: "Behold, I tell you a mystery." Then the Douay-Rheims, following the Latin Vulgate, reads: "We shall all indeed rise again: but we shall not all be changed."
Bibles translated from the Greek put it the other way round: we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed.

The copies of the letter differ here, and translators follow the text they have. Either way, Paul's point stands: in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet, the dead will rise incorruptible.
Then he borrows from the prophet Hosea and makes it a dare: "O death, where is thy victory? O death, where is thy sting?"
The Greek for sting is kentron: the stinger of a bee or a scorpion, and also the goad a farmer used to drive an ox. Paul names the stinger: the sting of death is sin.
Preachers sometimes add a picture: a bee that stings once leaves its stinger behind. In that picture, death stung Christ, and lost its sting. And Paul doesn't end with a final argument.

teach.h: THANKS BE TO GOD: THE VICTORY.
teach.b: He ends with thanks: "But thanks be to God, who hath given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ."
Catholics hear this chapter at funerals and confess it every Sunday in the Creed: I look forward to the resurrection of the dead.

teach.h: O DEATH, WHERE IS THY STING?
teach.b: The Church never pretends death doesn't hurt. A few verses earlier, Paul himself calls death an enemy, the last one to be destroyed. An enemy, but a beaten one.

how: Catholics pray for the dying, and the Church offers the anointing of the sick and Viaticum, a last Communion; 1 Corinthians 15 is among the readings for a Catholic funeral.

o: a stinger, like a bee's, or an ox-goad
a spear used to pierce the side
a crown of thorns worn in mockery

games.q: inside the chapter — tap the pairs.
p: a sting, or a farmer's goad

s: every manuscript of 1 Corinthians 15:51 reads the same
the Latin Vulgate, followed by the Douay-Rheims, reads it differently from the Greek text most modern Bibles follow.
1 Corinthians 15 is Paul's long defense of the resurrection of the dead
some in Corinth were saying the dead don't rise.
'where is thy sting' is Paul's own invention
he adapts it from the prophet Hosea.

games.q: some in Corinth say the dead don't rise. you're Paul, at the end of a long argument. how do you finish?
o: concede that only souls go on.
taunt death, and give thanks for the victory.
say it doesn't matter either way.
games.why: "O death, where is thy sting?" then: "thanks be to God, who hath given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ."

practice: Hold in mind someone who is dying, or very old, or very sick, someone you know or have only heard about; if that's too close today, think of everyone in the world who will die tonight, and picture them with care.
If you pray, use your own words, or the Hail Mary, which asks Mary to pray for us now and at the hour of our death. If you don't, wish them peace.

wordCard.voice: Kentron. The Greek word for a stinger or an ox-goad: Paul's taunt at death, whose sting, sin, Christ has drawn. Today's word.
